Binance began restoring customer withdrawals Sunday after hackers drained over $6 billion in the biggest cyber theft ever recorded, as the crypto industry awaits answers on the breach blamed on North Korea and steps to strengthen the exchange’s defenses.
The world’s largest digital-asset platform reopened Bitcoin withdrawals after 2 p.m. Singapore time, more than two days after halting them following the breach. By evening in Asia, the exchange had seen some $3.5 billion in net outflows, according to DefiLlama data. Co-Chief Executive Officer Yi He said on X some transfers are between Binance wallets.
The first phase of withdrawals covers 15 tokens, including Ether and the two biggest stablecoins, Tether’s USDT and Circle Internet Group Inc.’s USDC, Binance said on X. Withdrawals on 15 blockchain networks including Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, XRP and Base resumed by around 8:30 p.m. in Singapore, according to the company.
Read more: Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack: How Crypto Insurance Works
Binance dwarfs its industry rivals, with roughly $132 billion in assets, compared with about $29 billion at the second-largest exchange OKX. “We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened,” Binance said.
Quantitative trading firm SQS Trading has about a quarter of its trading capital on Binance, and is cutting that by roughly a third, according to founder Eli Williams, who added that it won’t flatten positions or reduce usage of the exchange as a venue for hedging. “It’s hard to forecast what the net impact will be at this point but we will be monitoring capital outflows and volume impact relative to other major venues,” Williams said.
Others are holding off any changes. Justin d’Anethan, head of research at Arctic Digital, a private markets advisory firm, said he’s not fazed by the hack. “When something seems fishy, it’s good to act fast; but when something catastrophic happens, it’s better to hold off doing anything,” he said. “I haven’t and wouldn’t move away from Binance.”
A spokesperson for Binance said the withdrawal volumes “spiked at the beginning,” but are now stabilizing to what the company considers normal activity, and a small percentage of its overall assets under management.
The restart tests Binance’s promise to make customers whole following a theft four times the size of the previous record crypto hack at Bybit in 2025. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation said on Saturday the Binance attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit it also held responsible for the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit theft.
The market fallout appears relatively contained, with most major cryptocurrencies seeing a change of less than 1% Sunday. Bitcoin, which accounts for about 60% of the sector’s market value, was trading around $78,000, about 5% below its Thursday high before the attack.
“On some level, this shows how much the industry has matured,” said Haseeb Qureshi, managing partner at venture fund Dragonfly. “We saw extraordinarily quick responses.”
Binance said it has so far replaced about 95% of the stolen cryptocurrency using its corporate treasury, emergency funds and insurance funds. The funds drained in the attack were a mix of the largest cryptocurrencies across 10 blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum.

It’s been a long and winding journey for Zouhair Talbi to realize his American dream, but winning the Houston Marathon in 2:05.45 on January 11 as a U.S. citizen was only part of that dream coming true.
The 31-year-old Moroccan-born runner ran the third-fastest time ever by a U.S. runner on a record-eligible course—behind only American record holder Conner Mantz (2:04:43 in Chicago last fall) and Khalid Khannouchi (2:05:38 in London in 2002)—taking nearly a minute off his personal best set two years earlier in Houston when he ran under his Moroccan citizenship in his lead-up to the Paris Olympics.
But not long after he celebrated at the finish line with an American flag draped over his shoulders, Zouhair relished another milestone moment as his wife, Elizabeth Talbi, 23, also had a breakthrough result in the marathon, placing 10th among women in 2:35:26—a 15-minute personal best from her debut effort in 2024—just 10 months after giving birth to their son, Amir.
Moreover, they each surpassed the qualifying standards for the 2028 U.S. Olympic Trials Marathon, which means they’ll both be on the starting line of the races that will determine who will make the U.S. team for the Los Angeles Olympics. The race will either be in Phoenix or St. Louis, and it is tentatively scheduled for the weekend of March 25-26, 2028. In other words, after August 2027, when Zouhair becomes eligible to officially compete for the U.S. in international races and national team qualifying events.
Best of all, they were also able to celebrate their success with Amir, who was cared for during the race by Elizabeth’s sister, Kaitlyn, who lives in Houston.
“It was a special day,” Zouhair said. “It was the first time I was listed as a U.S. runner with the American flag next to my name. It was something I had always dreamed of when I thought about coming to America. And to have Elizabeth run so well, too, really made it a special day for both of us.”
A Long and Winding Journey
Zouhair discovered his talent as a teen growing up in Tighassaline, Khenifra, Morocco, and emerged as one of the top high school runners in the country, eventually placing 14th in the U-20 race at the World Cross Country Championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland, as a 17-year-old in 2013. He continued on an upward trajectory as a college student, running 13:51 in the 5,000 meters as a 19-year-old and earning the silver medal in the event at the World University Games in Seoul, South Korea.
Despite his success, Zouhair says training and racing always seemed to be a constant struggle because of a lack of guidance and marginal support. He dreamed of running in the U.S. collegiate system, but it wasn’t until 2019, at the age of 23, that he enrolled at Florida State University.

She’s been on two Olympic teams and won the Boston Marathon, but Des Linden is still a rookie when it comes to ultra events.
In her first 100-miler, the Javelina Jundred on October 31 (stretching into November 1 for some runners) in Fountain Hills, Arizona, Linden finished as the ninth woman in 16 hours and 58 minutes.
Linden ran strongly for the first three laps of the five-lap race. She took over the lead at about the 40-mile mark and held onto that lead for the next 20 miles.
She hit 60.3 miles at 8:01:12, an average of 7:58 per mile pace for more than twice the marathon distance over the hilly trails.
But at the aid station at 60.3 miles, Linden sat down while her crew tended to her. She changed shoes and took about five minutes to get up and start running again. Within a half a mile of leaving the aid station, she was walking, and two female runners, Katie Asmuth and Carla Molinaro, passed her.
The final 40 miles took her 8 hours and 57 minutes.
Although the daylight hours were primarily dry on the desert loop, heavy rain drenched the course at the start and after night fell, drawing comparisons to the 2018 Boston Marathon, which Linden won, in a nor’easter.
The women’s race was incredibly close.
Heather Jackson, 42, won in 13:48:29, averaging 8:17 pace. Molinaro was second in 13:49:24, after Jackson overtook her in the final quarter mile of the race. Both earned “golden tickets” for the Western States Endurance Run, the famed 100-miler in June that goes from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California.
The men’s race was also close: Rob Molke, 35, finished in 12:11:30, holding off Noah Dusseau, who was runner-up in 12:12:57. They also earned “golden tickets” for Western States.
Linden will likely be motivated to solve the puzzle of the 100-mile distance, as she was early in her marathon career when she wanted to master 26.2 miles.
Her training wasn’t ideal leading up to Javelina, although she had several two-day stretches when she ran 30 miles one day and 20 the next.
She was aware she would need to adjust her goals if she started to struggle in the later miles.
“Just get to the finish. I think that’s super important,” she said in a phone interview with Runner’s World on October 29. “I think if I can run the whole time, that’s going to be great. And then if it’s going really well, I would love to get a golden ticket. But those are just as flexible as the plan. I know that even finishing can be something that all of a sudden comes into question. It’s just so different from anything I've done.”
Linden was also looking forward to the relaxed vibe and the chance to be around her crew and other runners.
“As a runner, you make these friends and they become your community,” she said. “But everyone lives [all over] the country. It’s hard to meet up with people, and so this is really just an excuse to hang out with a bunch of people who are really fun. It’ll be good. A good hang, no matter what.”

Ask any marathoner: There is nothing like the energy of race weekend to get you amped up to keep on running. Feeling the weight of that finisher’s medal hanging around your neck has a magical way of erasing all the aches and exhaustion you pushed through for the past few hours (not to mention the past several months of training).
But what you do in the hours and days immediately following 26.2 miles can determine how quickly you bounce back—not only physically but also how soon you’ll feel emotionally ready to get moving again. Marathons are draining, and that finish-line euphoria won’t keep sustaining you through continuous daily runs if you don’t let yourself recover fully.
After conquering 14 marathon finish lines in all seasons and a few back-to-back marathons too, I’ve learned a few key lessons about how to successfully get back to running postrace. Keep these in mind if you’ve just crossed a marathon off your list and want to lace up your running shoes again soon.
Don’t: Kick your feet up the entire rest of race day.
The first time I ran the New York City Marathon, I lived in a fifth-floor walk-up apartment on the Upper East Side. Going down those stairs the next day was excruciating, but I went outside anyway and went for a walk—and my legs felt immensely better a day later, compared with when I didn’t take those steps after other races.
Obviously, you should give yourself some downtime and relax after a marathon, but when I make a point to walk around more often right after a race and to do some other light activity (like easy pedaling on my Peloton) over the following few days, it always helps my legs feel way better sooner. Sitting on the couch all day will only increase your stiffness.
Do: Treat yourself!
Regardless of whether you hit a PR, qualified for Boston, or barely made it over the finish line, completing a marathon is a big accomplishment. I’ve found that taking some time after 26.2 to celebrate and appreciate my body for what it can do—and my mind for what it can push through—is an important step before jumping right back into running. When I push ahead without taking joy and pride in what I achieved, I wind up feeling run down and unmotivated.
If you feel like having a decadent meal and celebratory beers as part of that acknowledgment, Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect, says go for it! But to feel up to running again soon, have something nutritious first.
“The focus on recovery needs to be more dialed in if you're going to do another race soon,” he says. “That means nutrition and refueling a little more diligently. You can still enjoy pizza and beer, but make sure you get some protein and healthy carbs beforehand.”
Research backs this nutrient combo up: One 2018 study in Nutrients found that eating both carbs and protein immediately postrace helped marathoners’ physical fatigue, mental energy, and soreness improve within three days compared with those who ate carbs alone.
Don’t: Skimp on R&R.
Your body just did a lot; give it some extra TLC to help your muscles recover faster. Gaudette recommends trying out all the “little recovery tricks”—ice baths, dips in a hot tub, a massage—and seeing what helps you get back to 100 percent faster.

ExxonMobil (XOM +2.16%) just raised its quarterly dividend by another 3.9%, extending its growth streak to an industry-leading 44 consecutive years. That's a longer streak than 95% of companies in the S&P 500.
However, it was a very modest raise compared to its free cash flow, which has surged 90% year-over-year to $39 billion over the last nine months. That gap between the modest dividend increase and surging free cash flow isn't an accident, and what it says about how Exxon runs its cash is worth a closer look.
Image source: Getty Images.
Focused on the long term
ExxonMobil generated $19.1 billion in free cash flow during the third quarter alone, nearly as much as it produced during the first nine months of last year ($20.6 billion). That's enough cash to cover a year's worth of dividends with room to spare ($17.2 billion annually at its current $4.3 billion quarterly run rate). Clearly, Exxon has the capacity to deliver a much higher dividend increase.
However, the company's dividend payment is a fixed expense. Its cash flow, on the other hand, is highly variable. It has surged this year due to higher oil prices and refining margins caused by supply disruptions in the Middle East. When those disruptions finally ease, pricing and margins will fall, as will Exxon's free cash flow.

In his debut at the distance, Andreas Almgren ran today’s New York City Marathon like a veteran, perfectly marshaling his energy for one big move in the final mile to win in 2:06:01. The Swede is the first European man to win the race since Giacomo Leone in 1996.
Yeman Crippa of Italy, who was the last to hang with Almgren, placed second in 2:06:14 (and then promptly vomited). Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho outkicked defending champion Benson Kipruto in the final meters to finish third in a personal best of 2:06:26, one second ahead of Kipruto.
Zouhair Talbi, who occasionally took the lead between halfway and 30K (18.6 miles), was the top U.S. finisher, placing sixth in 2:06:43. In his debut marathon, Ahmed Muhumed was the second American, finishing seventh in 2:07:02. Ryan Ford was the third U.S. finisher, placing 10th in 2:07:17. Conner Mantz, running his first marathon since setting the U.S. record last year in Chicago, was 11th in 2:07:27.
Almgren is a world-class track runner—he won bronze at 10,000 meters at last year’s world championships—who has quickly also mastered road racing. Six weeks ago, he won the world half marathon championship in a national record of 58:06. He even boasts an 800-meter best of 1:45, a borderline world-class time that none of his competitors has run.
Despite that pedigree, none of the seasoned marathoners made a serious effort to drop Almgren far out from the finish. Fifteen men remained bunched at the 35K (21.7 miles) mark.
The real racing didn’t start until defending champ Kipruto surged to a 4:38 24th mile. That led to him, Almgren, and Crippa separating. Almgren, who trains by kilometers instead of miles, waited until just before 40K (24.9 miles) to take the lead for the first time. Crippa was able to stick with him for another kilometer, but right as Crippa snuck a look back on Central Park South, Almgren surged again and ran unchallenged to the finish.
When asked after the race whether he thought the moderate first 30 kilometers was playing into his hands, Almgren said, “Kinda, but not really. I mean, this is my first marathon. I don’t really know how it’s supposed to feel at those different points.”
At 20 miles, Almgren said, “I was like, ‘Shit, I’m tired. Why are my legs feeling like this?’” But a few minutes later, “I just started feeling like, ‘It’s pretty easy to respond now to the moves.’ So somewhere around there I felt like, ‘Okay, this might be my day.’”

Ciara Mageean, an Irish runner who set national records in the 800 meters, mile, and 1500 meters, died November 1, according to a social media post from her family. She was 34.
Mageean was diagnosed with stage 4 bowel cancer in May 2025.
She competed in two Olympics, in 2016 and 2021, in the 1500 meters, but she could not race at the Games in 2024, due to an Achilles injury.
The timing of that injury was unfortunate, because from 2023 to early 2024, Mageean was at the height of her powers.
In 2023, she ran personal bests in the mile (4:14.58) in June and 1500 meters (3:55.87) in September. That PR came en route to a victory at the Brussels Diamond League meet. In May of 2024, she ran 1:58.51 for 800 meters and the next month, she won the European Championships 1500 meters. Her final professional race was a Diamond League 2,000 meters in July 2024 in Monaco.
Mageean announced her cancer in a July 2025 post on Instagram, in which only her right arm, hooked up to a tube, was visible. The Olympic rings were tattooed on the inside of her wrist.
In June, Mageean released a book, My Greatest Race, about her cancer diagnosis. It became an all-Ireland bestseller.
Mageean was sponsored by New Balance, and at times, New Balance Boston athletes would cross paths with Mageean during altitude training stints in Flagstaff, Arizona. American miler Elle St. Pierre said she admired how tenacious Mageean was, training hard even when she couldn’t run due to injury.
“She was just very resilient,” St. Pierre said. “Through a number of injuries, she always came back so fast, and I feel like she she handled that mentally really well, too, and she’d still be training. That’s a really tough part of the sport, but something that really that stood out to me.”
Across the elite running world, athletes took to social media to pay tribute to Mageean, who had married Thomas Moran a few weeks ago in Belfast. Mageean posted photos from her wedding on Instagram six days ago.
Mark Coogan, coach of New Balance Boston, remembers enjoying a Guinness after the New Balance Indoor Games and laughing with Mageean.
“I saw her more as as a friend and someone to root for than someone that we were trying to beat all the time,” Coogan said.
Mageean set her mile national record in the race where Faith Kipyegon of Kenya set the world record.
“I will remember Ciara as a lovely person in and out of competition,” Kipyegon wrote on Instagram. “Simply an amazing person. I wish everyone around her strength in these difficult times.”
Síofra Cléirigh Büttner, who also ran for New Balance Boston and competed internationally for Ireland, plans to be in Dublin in December. She had texted Mageean just a few weeks ago to congratulate her on her wedding and suggest they have coffee. Mageean texted back, “I’d love to get coffee.”
Her death, Cléirigh Büttner said, feels sudden.
Mageean was a star from a young age, and instead of going to the U.S. for college and opting to run in the NCAA system, she stayed home in Ireland, with the backing of New Balance, and competed at home.
When Cléirigh Büttner was deciding what to do for college, Mageean came over for dinner one night to listen and offer her advice. “She was always just a very selfless person as well as just such a driven and ambitious and talented athlete,” Cléirigh Büttner said. (She decided to go to Villanova.)

Supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden reported sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers on Monday, sparking fears of a cyberattack similar to those that recently occurred in France.
Delhaize, which is owned by Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, confirmed that an “IT incident” took place at about 40 of its stores in Belgium on Sunday night, impacting the refrigeration systems, Belgian newswire Belga reported. A small number of Carrefour Belgium and Spar supermarkets also reported a similar issue, Belga said.
Several supermarkets of the ICA and Coop chains in Sweden are seeing higher temperatures in freezers, according to a report in newspaper Aftonbladet. The freezers’ temperature has been raised to 50C (122F), Ica Kvantum in Sjöbo, Sweden, said on its Facebook page, adding that it suspects a hack. Two more ICA stores are also reporting issues and Coop has six affected stores in the middle part of the country, Aftonbladet said.
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently providing support to these stores in managing the situation. We will provide further information when we can,” an ICA Sverige spokesperson told Bloomberg via email on Monday. The spokesperson didn’t confirm a cyberattack.
ICA has about a third of the Swedish grocery market, while Coop has about 17%.
The incidents raise concerns of a repeat of the disruption that took place in France last month, when 700 stores were hit by cyberattacks that disabled refrigeration systems and forced stores to throw out damaged food. The Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour SA chains were among those impacted. No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the hack.

The North Korean group accused of the world’s largest-ever crypto heist is a state-sponsored collective of elite hackers, groomed from an early age to hunt for “big game.” Artificial intelligence has now provided them with a powerful new tool to swell Kim Jong Un’s coffers and fund his military expansion.
Nuclear-armed North Korea maintains a thousands-strong hacker army, but the top unit known as “TraderTraitor”, which the FBI blames for the recent $6.3 billion Binance hack, may only have a dozen or so members, experts say.
Unlike garden-variety hackers targeting individual investors, TraderTraitor uses a strategy known as Big Game Hunting, cybersecurity experts say, helped by AI to seek out high-value crypto businesses to compromise. They’ve been so remarkably successful that the revenues they generate could be funding nearly half of North Korea’s banned weapons programs.
“This particular group looks for a big haul,” said Park Seong-su, Staff Threat Researcher at Zscaler, a cybersecurity firm. “They target crypto-related businesses, gain an understanding of their infrastructure and then tamper with it — or fund transfer processes — to execute a large-scale theft.”
With new AI tools “the barriers to such skills have dropped significantly, while the speed at which these operations can be carried out has increased tremendously,” Park added.
For decades, North Korea has picked its best and brightest students to join its hacking teams, training them at specialized institutions like Moranbong College in Pyongyang, defectors and experts say, to create an army which is now believed to be responsible for 89% of reported crypto hack losses this year, according to Chainalysis.
From running laptop farms in the US to stealing billions of crypto in less than 30 minutes, its hackers have become one of the most important sources of revenue for North Korea, which is isolated from the global financial system due to rafts of sanctions over Kim’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.
North Korea’s other income sources, such as trade with China and even the military relationship with Russia, are now dwarfed in significance by crypto cash. Once, Pyongyang was smuggling cigarettes and forging US dollar bills to stay afloat — now its hackers bring in billions in pure profit from a single successful heist.
And it could be getting worse, thanks to AI.

Crypto exchanges are beefing up security, especially for employees with key access, to protect against TraderTraitor’s modus operandi: combining top-tier hacking skills with social engineering. They have been known to identify employees with high-level access to target systems and aggressively pursue them with things like lucrative job offers, said Carlsen.
“Their bread and butter is the human part,” he said.
Binance has said an initial investigation found a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer as a point of breach. Five questions about Missouri’s election. Some are easier to answer than others.
From abortion rights and redistricting to competitive races in the suburbs, Tuesday’s election could offer clues about where Missouri politics is headed
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Missouri voters keep rejecting some of the GOP’s biggest ideas. Then they keep electing Republicans to run the state.
Two years ago, voters protected abortion rights and approved paid sick leave. In August, they overwhelmingly rejected proposals to overhaul the tax system and make constitutional amendments harder to pass.
Yet Republicans hold every statewide elected office, six of eight congressional seats and supermajorities in both legislative chambers.
On Tuesday, voters will revisit several of those disagreements. Here are five questions I’m watching.
1. Didn’t we already settle the abortion question?
You’d think so.
In 2024, voters approved Amendment 3, enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution. Republican lawmakers responded by putting another amendment on the ballot.
So we’re doing this again?
Yes, but not quite the same way.
Amendment 3 would repeal those protections and restore a ban on most abortions, with limited exceptions. It would also constitutionally prohibit gender-affirming medical care for minors.
Wait, it’s also Amendment 3?
Yes. Missouri recycles amendment numbers. Political arguments, too.
This time around, a yes vote bans abortion and a no vote keeps it legal.
What do the polls say?
An August SLU/YouGov poll found 43% in favor, 44% opposed and 13% undecided.
A small but vocal minority of anti-abortion activists oppose the amendment, arguing the proposed ban doesn’t go far enough. Meanwhile, Amendment 3’s supporters have mounted a more organized campaign than they did two years ago, particularly through churches working to mobilize voters.
The question is whether the coalition that protected abortion rights in 2024 will hold together in the face of that effort.
2. Can Ann Wagner survive another Democratic wave?
Wagner has seen this movie before.
In 2018, Democrats gained dozens of U.S. House seats. Wagner survived, winning her suburban St. Louis district by about four points. She’s won every election since.
At some point, Democrats might wonder whether the district is actually competitive or just enjoys making them think it is.
So why is this year different?
An October Emerson College poll showed Democratic challenger Fred Wellman leading Wagner 51% to 46%. Other surveys have shown tighter margins.
Last week, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the district from leaning Republican to a toss-up. The result could offer a window into whether the suburban backlash against Republicans that defined 2018 is returning eight years later.
3. Is Missouri’s redistricting fight finally over?
That depends on your definition of over.
After more than a year of Republican maneuvering and courtroom battles, the gerrymandered version of Missouri’s congressional map is finally on the ballot. The GOP-drawn map, designed to help Republicans win seven of eight U.S. House seats, won’t be used Tuesday.
But Proposition A will determine its fate in future elections.
Remind me how that works.
A yes vote approves the Republican-drawn map for future elections. A no vote rejects it.
So a no vote ends the whole thing?
Not necessarily.

A bridge stretches across the Missouri River at Chamberlain, South Dakota, on Sept. 29 (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight).
Downstream Missouri River states have worried for decades about receiving an insufficient flow of water from upstream dams.
Now they’re worried their share of water could be further diminished by potential pipelines for dry Western states.
The concern is the basis of a dispute about the U.S. House version of the federal Water Resources Development Act. A provision in the bill would require approval from all governors in Missouri River states to study or construct a project that moves water from the river or its tributaries to a non-Missouri River state.
The bill has passed the House and awaits action in the Senate, where a Senate version of the legislation lacks the controversial provision.
Missouri lawmaker and group support provision
The House bill’s definition of “Missouri River states” includes not only the seven states where the river flows — Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas and Missouri — but also Colorado, Minnesota and Wyoming, which have land within the river’s 530,000-square-mile drainage basin.
A downstream lawmaker, U.S. Rep. Sam Graves, R-Missouri, sponsors the House bill. Supporters of the controversial provision include an organization in his state, the Coalition to Protect the Missouri River.
Shane Kinne is the coalition’s executive director. He said Missourians’ concerns about water shortages are not hypothetical. For the last four years, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has limited water releases from upper Missouri River reservoirs, affecting commercial barge traffic downstream.
Kinne said Missouri River Basin states should collaborate “so we can manage the resource together and protect ourselves from Western states looking for water.”
“If this isn’t the proposal, let’s bring some ideas to address this concern,” he said.
Joint opposition: Dakotas, Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah
Kinne’s view faces opposition in upstream states.
The governors of Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota — where the Missouri River flows through a series of dams and reservoirs — recently joined with governors in the Missouri River Basin states of Colorado and Wyoming on a letter opposing the House provision.
Also signing the letter was the governor of Utah, which is not part of the Missouri River Basin. Utah relies on the Colorado River for some of its water, and the state’s Great Salt Lake Commission has mentioned the Missouri River as a potential source of imported water for the vanishing Great Salt Lake.

"The housing market is haunted," according to David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management.
He lists the ghosts in his widely read Oct. 26 research note: more than a decade of too-easy money, tariffs, and immigration policies that raise the cost of building homes while limiting the number of people who need them, and a Fed whose rate swings hit housing harder than almost anything else.
The one that should get the most attention is the people who aren't showing up. Kelly said he expects U.S. population growth of just 800,000 a year over the next few years. With an average household of about 2.5 people, he writes, that "implies a demographic need for just 320,000 new housing units per year," compared with roughly 1 million per year in the first two decades of this century.
That cuts against the story most Americans have heard about housing: that the country simply hasn't built enough. Zillow estimated in July the U.S. was about 4.7 million homes short as of 2024, based on how many families are doubled up with unrelated people compared with how many homes sit vacant for rent or sale. Kelly's read is that the country is "still in a situation of net excess supply."
Thursday's GDP report bore that out, Kelly told Fortune by email. Homebuilding fell again in the third quarter, "marking the 8th decline in residential construction in the last 10 quarters." But "the homebuilding decline is still relatively modest compared to the very fast increase in AI-related capital spending," he said.
Where the people went
In the first 20 years of this century, Kelly wrote, the U.S. population grew by an average of 2.4 million people a year—about 1.5 million from births minus deaths and about 900,000 from net immigration. The natural increase peaked at 520,000 in 2025, he writes, and has likely resumed a steady decline as the population ages and birth rates fall.
Immigration swung harder. Net international migration fell to 1.3 million in the year through July 2025 from 2.7 million a year earlier, and the Census Bureau projected it would be about 321,000 by July 2026 if trends continued. Kelly estimated that deportations are now almost canceling out legal net immigration, which is still positive but smaller. He said he expects that to hold "regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections," because enforcement is largely up to the administration, and Congress and the White House are unlikely to agree on an immigration reform bill.
The empty-house signs
Kelly pointed to vacancies. Over the past four years, he writes, the rental vacancy rate rose from 5.6% to 7.3%, and the homeowner vacancy rate from 0.8% to 1.2%. Census figures released Wednesday put rental vacancy at 7.6% in the third quarter, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Between the second quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026, he writes, the housing stock grew by about 2.8 million units.
Buyers have thinned out. Many runners think of the climbs as the toughest part of a hilly race. Uphills send your heart rate soaring and slow even the strongest runners to a grind, while descents offer a chance to catch your breath and let gravity do some of the work. But David Roche, ultramarathoner and coach to New York City Marathon women’s runner-up Jess McClain, says those easier-feeling downhills can come at a cost later in the race.
And Roche knows the importance of late-race performance, which is why he integrates strategies into his training to fight fatigue through long distances.
Take McClain’s finish in New York City as an example: She outkicked reigning champ Hellen Obiri just feet from the finish line to take second place by mere seconds, clocking 2:24:42 and becoming the first American woman to reach the podium in NYC since 2018.
Roche’s fatigue-fighting tactics take him even farther in his own races. The two-time Life Time Leadville 100 winner—and course record holder—covered the famously demanding trails in 15:12:30, averaging roughly 9:07 per mile. Yet he rarely relies on extremely long, arduous training runs to prepare for conquering late miles.
Instead, Roche uses downhill workouts to reproduce some of the muscular stress that can cause runners’ legs to fail in an endurance event. “Downhills are the gateway to fatigue resistance in these really long events,” Roche tells Runner’s World.
The best part is, you don’t have to be an elite like McClain or Roche to benefit from his advice. He shares how purposeful downhill training can help runners preserve their strength, form, and pace deep into a race. Plus, he offers his go-to workout to add to your buildup.
Why Downhill Training Is an Underrated Durability Booster
Running downhill may provide some relief to your cardiovascular system—by lowering your heart rate a bit as gravity naturally carries you downward—but it puts much more strain on your musculoskeletal system. To keep you from tumbling down the hill, the quads must repeatedly brake the body’s momentum.
Braking action involves eccentric contractions, meaning the muscles produce force while lengthening under load, Roche explains. Eccentric contractions occur during many activities—including simply walking down stairs—but running a lengthy descent can deliver thousands in succession, significantly increasing the load on your muscles.
When the body isn’t accustomed to the stress caused by downhill running, the aftermath can wreck you. Roche explains that while a runner may feel relatively normal after their first downhill running workout, they end up developing significant soreness within a day or two. “That feeling of, ‘Oh man, I have no quads right now,’ a few days later is also what happens to your quads in an ultra,” Roche says—and even a marathon.
The initial downhill running effort, however, also triggers an adaptation known as the repeated bout effect. A review published in 2024 on the subject describes the repeated bout effect as a form of skeletal-muscle memory in which the first eccentric challenge activates protective responses that make the muscle more resistant to damage than subsequent ones.

By all accounts, it was a perfect day to go for a run.
On the first Sunday morning in October 1972, Central Park was bathed in early fall sunshine, the crisp 50-degree air giving the changing leaves on the sugar maples and Sawtooth oaks near Tavern on the Green a bit of a sheen as the third New York City Marathon was scheduled to go off. It doesn’t feel right using an uppercase M with this marathon. At the time, the race was decidedly small-scale. Only 278 runners had signed up (for this year’s race on November 4, some 47,000 have entered), they paid just $1 to get in (instead of today’s $255), and the entire 26.2-mile race took place within the confines of the park, whereas today’s marathon stretches over five boroughs and requires the space of Central Park just to stage the start. And Fred Lebow, who would ultimately become the impresario of the world’s largest race, had yet to make a name for himself beyond the city’s small and chummy running fraternity.
But perhaps suggestive of his P.T. Barnum–like skills, Lebow had persuaded The New York Times and a few other dailies to come to the park that day. News, Lebow promised, would happen. So the Times sent one of its reporters, Gerald Eskenazi, to cover the race, and Patrick Burns, a Times photographer for nearly 50 years, to shoot it.
And, as promised, something happened, without a single running step being taken.
Shortly before 11 a.m., the six women entered in the race—yes, just six—lined up at the start. Lebow and his fellow organizers had openly courted women when the first New York City Marathon was held in 1970, even going so far as to ignore rules put in place by the Amateur Athletic Union that barred women from marathon race courses. For years the AAU, the then-governing body of track and field and distance running and which sanctioned events such as marathons, had been intent on smothering a bubbling interest among women who wanted to run longer and race farther. It did so by disseminating unfounded “scientific” research (for instance, that women who ran more than a few miles risked infertility) and invoking confounding rules to keep women on the sidelines.
But soon after the second New York City Marathon, in the fall of 1971, the AAU relented, somewhat, on its stance: It ruled that “certain women” could take part in marathons, provided they either start their race 10 minutes before or after the men or on a different starting line. The rulings—imposed so women would run a “separate but equal” race from the men—were viewed by many runners of the day, female and male alike, as just the latest act of discrimination enacted by the AAU.
Five of the six women on the Central Park starting line came from either Manhattan or Long Island. Their running résumés varied to the extreme: One woman had won the Boston Marathon five months earlier; another rarely ran at all. Dear New York City,
Probably the most excruciating breath I’ve taken in my life was in Lenox Hill Hospital on East 77th Street. It was my first breath on Earth, and my lungs must have wondered what had hit them. Forty-three years later, it seemed fitting that I’d come back to you for another challenge to my lungs and body: my first marathon.
I have lots of memories of you, starting from those early years on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Then there were holiday visits and sleepovers with my grandmother in Stuyvesant Town, special days in Dad’s office in Washington Heights, Mom’s gallery openings in the Village. There were the fits and starts of my early professional career when I lived in Brooklyn and then Alphabet City, using most of my paycheck for rent, the rest for food. And of course, after I moved away in my late 20s, when I’d see you a couple of times a month for work.
If I’m being honest, you’ve always been a bit of a headache and a challenge. Back when I was just starting out, I couldn’t tolerate your high prices and abrasive attitude, and your tendency to “never sleep.” Which is why I ditched you for a less exhausting life in the country. Even today, I stress out just thinking about seeing you.
But on an unseasonably warm November Sunday, NYC Marathon day, you challenged me more than ever before—and revealed a level of grit I didn’t know was in me.
On the Verrazzano Bridge, I was overcome with emotion at having made it to the starting line. Surrounded by scores of runners from all over the world, with the open waterway below and the iconic skyline in the distance, I felt like a part of something huge and meaningful. It literally brought tears to my eyes.
Running through Brooklyn, I was in a zone. I was able to stay on pace and hit the halfway mark in decent shape, so I forced a smile at the throngs of cheering spectators. I’ve never been one to smile during races, and even your generous Brooklynites couldn’t get me to light up a genuine grin.
Then came the 59th Street Bridge. Long Island City, with its dull stretches of low-slung warehouses, is perhaps one of your most charmless neighborhoods. Nothing against the spectators who did their best in the streets leading up to the bridge, but that endless, gradual incline in the eerie quiet with the wind blowing up off the East River is where I started to unravel.
The screaming wall of people on First Avenue did nothing to energize me. This is where I began to feel like perhaps a marathon is just too long a run to be considered a wise choice.
And, sorry. Even if the Bronx had welcomed me with confetti and a marching band, it wouldn’t have mattered. Once I got to the Willis Avenue Bridge, I regretted not bringing money or a MetroCard so I could duck out and just go home. With every step, my feet, my quads, my knees threatened imminent shutdown. Worse was the shivering that seemed to consume my whole body, like when you lie feverish in bed, begging for the Tylenol to kick in.
Harlem was a fleeting boost, lifting me up ever so briefly at Mile 22 with its gospel choir, its Jamaican ska, its salsa beat. New York, here is where you started to shine and where I started to believe in myself. Your Harlem spectators literally reached out their hands and told me, “You can do this” and “You look strong.” They warmed me with their smiles when my body was wracked with chills. They let me pet their Bernese Mountain Dog, a wagging gift of comfort when all I wanted was to curl up on the sidewalk.

You’ve crossed the finish line, collected your medal, and celebrated a goal that once demanded months of early mornings and long runs. Now comes the less glamorous part of the marathon: recovery.
You might be eager to get back on the road—or perfectly happy to take a break. Either way, the days and weeks after a marathon deserve as much thought as the training that got you to the starting line in the first place.
Here’s how to decide how long to rest, recognize when you’re ready to return, and ease back into training so you can build toward your next goal feeling strong.
How to Determine How Long to Rest After a Marathon
Exactly when you return to running after a marathon depends on how the race went, your overall effort during it, and how you feel. Some experts recommend one day of recovery time for every mile raced—so 26 days of rest for marathoners. And some even recommend one day of rest for each kilometer raced, which would mean 42 days of recovery.
Don’t panic, though! The good news is that “rest” does not have to mean no running at all (though it can). It just means taking a break from high-intensity training such as speedwork or other races.
Remember, running a race at a submaximal effort is different than racing it at a high effort. But either way, there’s no exact formula to follow for recovery after a marathon, so the best guide is really tuning in and listening to your body.
At a minimum, take three to seven days completely off from running after a marathon. Sleep in, eat, and enjoy your accomplishment. After that, begin an active recovery program. Active recovery includes light exercise and can include some running, if you are not sore and feel mentally and physically ready to get back to it.
More specifically, “light” exercise means exercising at a low-intensity level, i.e., no more than 60 to 65 percent of your max heart rate for a relatively short duration, like less than 60 minutes. Activity actually helps you recover faster than inactivity because it promotes circulation. And good circulation delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to muscles and carries away metabolic waste and, therefore, aids healing and recovery.
If you do want to clock miles, focus on recovery runs during this time—keeping the effort light and easy, meaning you should be able to have a conversation the entire time you’re running.
Signs You’re Recovering From Your Marathon
Your body will let you know when it wants to run again, and one message it will send is through soreness. Minimal soreness is a good sign because it means your body is recovering from the challenge, but it may take a few days to kick in.
Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically follows most marathon efforts. The soreness results from microscopic muscle tissue damage, and the severity of it depends on your fitness level and the intensity of the effort relative to the training effort. The degree of soreness indicates the extent of muscle damage, and this will influence the duration of your recovery period.
In other words, the more soreness, the longer the recovery. (A lack of soreness indicates you were well prepared for the demands of your race, so good job with your training.) When the soreness subsides, that’s an indicator that you’re ready for action again.

All three banks released third-quarter results in mid-October, offering updates on their finances and their future plans. Which ones have actually followed through on these share repurchase agreements, shrinking their share count and giving investors more bang for their investment buck?
JPMorgan has the biggest buyback but the slowest pace
In June 2026, JPMorgan's board authorized a new $50 billion common stock repurchase program, effective July 1. And during the third quarter, JPMorgan repurchased around $1 billion in common stock but recorded only $664 million in net repurchases. In other words, that gross amount used only about 2% of the new authorization.

Management has emphasized that repurchases must compete with other uses of capital, including investments in the business, lending opportunities, and the maintenance of a strong balance sheet. The bank also faces risks around weaker credit quality and investment banking activity.

Snap Inc. is finalizing a settlement in a lawsuit filed by two teenagers who say years of compulsive scrolling and posting on the company’s photo-sharing app contributed to their mental health struggles, according to attorneys for the plaintiffs.
The agreement, reached partway through jury selection in Los Angeles, would enable the company to avoid the next high-profile social media addiction trial. The case in California state court was set to be the latest test of thousands of such lawsuits. The teenagers previously reached confidential settlements with Meta Platforms Inc., TikTok and Google’s YouTube.
“Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal,” John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, attorneys for one of the teens, said in a statement announcing the agreement. Terms of the settlement weren’t disclosed.
Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply
The two cases, which were combined by the judge, would have been the second to go to trial among thousands of lawsuits filed by young users and their family members accusing the social media companies of engineering their platforms to profit at the expense of young people’s safety and mental health.
The companies deny these allegations and stress that they have rolled out tools and resources to support parents with teens on the platform. They’ve also sought to highlight positive experiences that users have online.
Snap didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The teenage plaintiffs in the case that was scheduled to go to trial this week are identified in court documents as S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi. Both claim their heavy use of Snapchat and other social media platforms caused and contributed to their depression, anxiety and eating disorders.
Related: Meta Settles With Teen During Trial Testing Claims Social Media Caused Depression, Eating Disorders
Families shouldn’t have to seek jury trials “to solve a problem this big,” Mark Lanier, the plaintiffs’ trial counsel for the case, said in a statement. “What these teenagers need is a permanent fix, real design changes that protect kids, not case-by-case patches. Until that happens, we will keep trying these cases.”
S.J. and K.D.B.’s lawsuits were selected from the larger pool of litigation to serve as so-called bellwether cases. The outcomes of these early trials could encourage broader settlement talks by showing lawyers the strengths and weaknesses of their arguments and evidence — and ultimately how much the remaining cases are worth.
The first bellwether case went to trial earlier this year against Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google. A 20-year-old woman was awarded $6 million after a jury found the companies were negligent in the design and operation of their platforms and should have warned that their products could harm young users. Snap and TikTok reached confidential settlement agreements with the woman before that trial.

When people find out I broke my leg in several places, the first question they ask is, “How did it happen?” I wish I had a great story to tell, but here’s the truth: I broke it slowly, over many miles, as I trained for a fall marathon.
After running the London Marathon this year, I took a few weeks off to recover before I started training for Chicago. I planned on following a 16-week training plan, but because I had taken some time off, I slowly began building my base back up three weeks before the official start of my plan.
Everything went great to start. The hip pain that ailed me in the winter disappeared and my legs felt fresh. I ran a few 4-milers to gauge my fitness level, and I was shocked when I almost scored a personal best. After the second 4-miler, I felt a slight pain in my shin. I’ve had shin splints before, so I thought nothing of it. After a few more weeks of consistent running, though, the pain grew so severe that I pulled back on my running to let my shin heal.
After a month of never-ending pain, I went to the doctor for an expert opinion. After a round of X-rays, the doctor told me the issue was probably shin splints and that I could slowly return to running. I asked whether it could be a stress fracture because the pain felt more intense than a normal shin splint, but was assured my leg was fine.
Three days later at a concert at Red Rocks Amphitheater in Colorado, I turned to say hi to a friend and felt a pop. I immediately knew that I broke my leg. A rod, plate, and seven screws later, I’m now sidelined from running for months, if not longer.
Turns out, I probably did have a stress fracture–but they are hard to detect on X-rays. In fact, Runner’s World published this a story the week before my injury that details how stress fractures are “notoriously tricky to diagnose.” Our story also goes through the five stress fracture warning signs you need to pay attention to. And looking back, I checked off every box, from discomfort with activity to pain that increased throughout runs.
As runners, we know our bodies, and we know when something isn’t right. I regret not getting a second expert opinion on my leg pain. That’s my biggest takeaway from this ordeal. If something feels off, investigate it and ask a lot of questions. Don’t be afraid to be annoying. Trusting your gut is better than being holed up with a broken leg.
I know I will come back stronger than before. Not being able to run makes me appreciate it so much more. Looking back at my previous training blocks, I also know that going forward, I am going to make smarter choices. I should have added more mobility and strength training into my plan to help me reduce my injury risk. Right before sustaining my injury, Runner’s World released the comprehensive Guide to Strength Training program, and I had started completing–and loving–the six follow-along workouts provided in the guide. I can’t wait to get back to them when I’m healed.
